ety.text: From Middle English ynke, from Old French enque, from Latin encaustum (“purple ink used by Roman emperors to sign documents”), from Ancient Greek ἔγκαυστον (énkauston, “burned-in”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + καίω (kaíō, “burn”). In this sense, displaced native Old English blæc (“ink”, literally “black”). Sense four refers to the ink used in newspapers.

senses.d: A pigment (or dye)-based fluid used for writing, printing etc.
ex: This form should be filled out in ink.

senses.d: A particular type, color or container of this fluid.
